Sioux Falls housing at a glance

Sioux Falls is South Dakota's largest city and the Minnehaha County seat, and a northern edge of town spills into Lincoln County. The city sits near the Minnesota line, where Interstate 29 meets Interstate 90. The 2020 census counted 192,517 residents, a jump of 25.1 percent over the decade. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 213,748.

Growth this fast means new subdivisions keep going up and compete with older neighborhoods for the same buyers. Health care, banking and food processing are the big employers, led by Sanford Health and Avera Health. When someone is moved or hired by one of them, the old house often has to sell quickly, and a start date will not wait for a slow listing.

Flood rules for Sioux Falls houses

If your house is in a mapped floodplain, extra permit rules apply, and the city enforces them once storms do damage. Following the flash flooding of June 2024, Planning and Development Services reminded owners that construction or repair in a floodplain requires a floodplain development permit even when no building permit would be needed.

The city adds up damage over three years. Once repair costs hit 45 percent or more of the structure's pre-flood market value, work cannot begin until the owner shows the floodplain ordinance is met, which may mean elevating or flood-proofing the building. If your house is flood damaged, call the city about where that line falls before paying a contractor.

On insurance, the city moved to Community Rating System Class 7 on October 1, 2023, which gives 15 percent off National Flood Insurance Program premiums on covered properties. The city announcement has the current class.

Rental permits

Anyone who owns or manages a rental in Sioux Falls, long or short term, needs a city rental permit as of January 1, 2024, including people who registered before then. The permit costs $50 per address, and the owner completes a one-time training course of at least two hours.

  • Get the permit before advertising, soliciting renters or allowing anyone to move in.
  • Each rental street address needs its own permit.
  • Tell the city in writing within 30 days if ownership or management changes.
  • Owners who live over 50 miles out need a local contact for upkeep.
  • A fourth violation can lead to revocation when three were cited in the previous three calendar years.

Transferring a permit costs nothing when written notice is given, so tell the buyer of a tenant-occupied house to file that notice. Code Enforcement also handles nuisance, property maintenance, signs, trees, grass, weeds and zoning complaints, which means a tall lawn or a debris pile can draw a citation before closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Sioux Falls house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Seller paperwork in South Dakota

Expect three items at nearly every closing: the seller's disclosure, the Certificate of Real Estate Value and the transfer fee. The disclosure is a state form dated 07/2025, and the law says the buyer must receive it. Its questions run through liens, easements, flood plains, the roof, water penetration, radon, lead paint, mold and about 47 systems and appliances. Put any change in a material fact in writing before closing.

The PT 56 Certificate of Real Estate Value has to travel with the deed. It names both parties, describes the land and states the true price and terms.

Document or feeMinnehaha County amount or rule
Recording a deed$30.00
Transfer fee$1.00 per thousand ($0.50 per $500)
Exemptions from the fee19, listed in SDCL 43-4-22
PT 56 certificateNeeded for any deed or contract for deed

Houses on the Lincoln County side are recorded in that county instead. Your tax bill shows which county applies, so look before you set a closing date.

Taxes owed at closing

Because the state bills a year in arrears, sellers typically owe a share of the current bill when they close. In Minnehaha County the due date is January 1. You can pay the first half penalty-free through April 30 and the second through October 31. After that a 10 percent annual penalty applies. Whatever is unpaid is taken from your proceeds, and the treasurer will quote the payoff.

Owner-occupied status lowers the rate, but only if the owner lives in the home on the November 1 assessment date. A buyer who moves in after a sale applies between November 1 and March 15. Our Sioux Falls property tax guide goes deeper on assessments and levies.

Winter and your inspection

Sioux Falls winters are cold, bringing about 25 days a year at or below zero and about 45.3 inches of snow. Repeated freezing and thawing damages shingles, gutters, walks and foundation walls. A buyer using a mortgage may ask you to fix a tired roof or a wet basement. Before any showing, walk the attic, the basement walls and the gutters, and fix or at least list what you find, since inspectors in this climate look at those first. A cash buyer generally takes those items as they are, one reason owners of houses with deferred maintenance consider that route.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Sioux Falls houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which way of selling fits you?

Hiring an agent normally exposes the house to the most buyers, at the price of showings, inspections, repair demands and a commission. Going solo saves the commission but puts all the paperwork on you. Cash tends to win when the problem is time, condition or tenants.

  • An inherited house with an unfinished estate
  • A rental with tenants or an unresolved permit problem
  • Flood or storm damage you cannot afford to repair
  • Back taxes or a mortgage slipping behind
  • A relocation with a fixed start date

We buy Sioux Falls houses as-is. Offers depend on the property, and you can decline at no cost.

What a cash sale skips

A cash purchase removes the appraisal, the lender's underwriting and the haggling over repairs. After you describe the house and we make an offer, a title company checks ownership, clears liens and prepares the papers, and you set the closing date. Before then, find the deed or legal description, the tax notice, any rental permit number and mortgage payoff details. A tenant in the house means we need the lease terms from the start, including the end date and deposit.

Closing costs and back taxes come out of the proceeds, so nothing is due from you at the table.

Frequently asked questions

How big is Sioux Falls?

The Census Bureau estimates 213,748 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 192,517 in 2020. It is the state's largest city.

Does a Sioux Falls seller have to give a disclosure statement?

Yes. South Dakota requires sellers of real property to complete the property condition disclosure and give it to the buyer. Amend it in writing if a material fact changes before closing.

What is the transfer fee in Minnehaha County?

The county lists $1.00 per thousand, or $0.50 per $500, plus a $30.00 recording fee for a deed. SDCL 43-4-22 lists 19 exemptions, such as some transfers between spouses or parent and child.

Do I need a rental permit to sell a tenant-occupied house?

The owner must hold a city permit at $50 per address. It transfers without a fee when written notice is given, and ownership changes must be reported within 30 days.

Can I sell with back property tax due, and which county do I pay?

Yes. Unpaid tax and the 10 percent annual penalty are paid from proceeds at closing. Most of the city is in Minnehaha County and a smaller part is in Lincoln County, so check your tax notice for the right treasurer.

Rapid City housing at a glance

Rapid City is the Pennington County seat, on the eastern slope of the Black Hills. The 2020 census counted 74,703 residents, and the metro area holds about 156,000. That makes it South Dakota's second-largest city.

The city is split by a low ridge called The Gap and by the Dakota Hogback. The Westside lies in the Red Valley, while the central and eastern neighborhoods sit in the Rapid Creek valley. Newer building has crept into the foothills and north along Interstate 90. A foothill house and a creekside house carry very different risks, so where the property sits drives both value and repair needs.

Government, health care and tourism lead local employment. Ellsworth Air Force Base, home of the 28th Bomb Wing, brings steady transfers in and out. A seller with military orders often has to close on a fixed date, which is hard with a listing that depends on a buyer's loan.

Flood rules for a Rapid City property

A parcel in a Special Flood Hazard Area falls under FEMA rules and city permits. Rapid City takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program. The June 1972 Black Hills Flood is the reason the city enforces floodplain permitting so strictly: it killed 238 people and destroyed or damaged 1,335 homes.

To find out whether a house is in the 100-year floodplain, meaning a 1 percent chance of flooding in any year, call the city's Floodplain Administrator at 394-4154. FEMA issued new maps for Pennington County on June 3, 2013, and the city's Floodplain Management page lists later map revisions.

  • Building or repairing inside the floodplain requires a Floodplain Development Permit.
  • The rules sit in Rapid City Municipal Code chapters 15.32 and 17.28.
  • An elevation certificate documents a structure's height for insurance.

A buyer who needs flood insurance will ask for these answers, so have them ready. Details are on the city's Floodplain Management page.

Vacation rental rules

Rapid City council passed its first zoning rules for vacation homes on December 2, 2025, by an 8 to 2 vote under Ordinance No. 6698. Registration is open for owners who operate one. A vacation home is a whole dwelling rented to the public for up to 28 consecutive days and more than 14 days a year, with no owner or manager living there during the rental.

  • Up to five bedrooms is a permitted use in the listed districts.
  • More than five bedrooms needs a conditional use permit.
  • Occupancy is capped at two people per bedroom plus two more.
  • Parking must be provided, and operators need a South Dakota lodging license.

If your house has been a short-term rental, make sure the registration is current. A buyer may ask for the city registration number and the state license, and the answer affects what the house is worth to an investor.

Pennington County property tax dates

Pennington County bills in arrears. The assessment notice arrives on or near March 1, and the value reflects the market as of the previous November 1.

EventDateWhat it means

First halfAfter April 30Delinquent past this date
Second halfAfter October 31Delinquent past this date
Special assessmentsBefore May 1Due in full; mortgage companies do not always pay them
Monthly ACH planApply by December 15Ten payments, for the following year

Homestead deferral and the assessment freeze

Two relief programs matter at sale time. The Homestead Exemption defers taxes until the property is sold, so the deferred taxes plus interest come out of your proceeds at closing. The Assessment Freeze for seniors and disabled owners needs an application by April 1.

The Department of Revenue also lists a municipal property tax reduction for elderly and disabled Rapid City residents. Call the Treasurer's Office at 605-394-2163 to ask how a sale changes any benefit you receive, and request a payoff figure before you sign anything.

Selling a house in the floodplain

A flood-zone address is not a dead end, but it narrows the buyer pool. Some buyers need flood insurance for their loan, and the premium can scare them off. Sellers do better when they show up with paperwork: the elevation certificate if one exists, any permits for past repairs, and a record of how the house has handled heavy rain.

Be straight on the disclosure form. It asks about flood plains directly, and a wrong answer can come back after closing. If repairs are needed and you cannot fund them, a buyer who purchases as-is removes that problem from your plate.

Weather and your inspection

Rapid City is drier than the eastern part of the state, with hot summers and long winters. Snow load, fast temperature swings and summer sun wear on roofs, siding and decks. Older houses in the Rapid Creek valley and on the Westside often still have original windows and aging heating systems, and a buyer's inspector will point them out. Fix the cheap items first, and gather service records for the furnace and roof so buyers see a house that was maintained and cared for over the years.

Paperwork for a Rapid City sale

Every South Dakota seller must hand the buyer a completed property condition disclosure statement. The form is dated 07/2025 and covers liens, easements, flood plains, roof leaks, radon, lead paint, mold and whether systems work. If a material fact changes before closing, a written amendment is required.

A Certificate of Real Estate Value (PT 56) must accompany the deed for it to be recorded. The transfer fee is set by SDCL 43-4-21, and SDCL 43-4-22 lists 19 exemptions, among them some transfers between spouses and between parent and child for nominal consideration. For comparison, Minnehaha County charges $1.00 per thousand. The Pennington County Register of Deeds will quote the figure for your sale.

How a cash sale works in Rapid City

A cash sale fits when a deadline, a repair bill or a title problem makes a standard listing hard. Around here that often means flood-zone houses, military moves, inherited homes and former vacation rentals.

We buy Rapid City houses as-is. We make no promises on price before we see the property, and you owe nothing if you turn the offer down.

The steps are short. You share the address and condition, we inspect, and we make an offer. If you agree, a title company confirms ownership, clears liens and sets the closing date you choose. A cash buyer skips the appraisal and loan underwriting that can delay a conventional sale. Bring your tax notice, any flood paperwork, and for a rental the registration and lodging license. Any deferred homestead taxes or unpaid assessments are settled from the proceeds.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in Rapid City?

The 2020 census counted 74,703 residents. The Census Bureau estimates 80,589 as of July 1, 2025.

Is my Rapid City house in a floodplain?

Call the city's Floodplain Administrator at 394-4154 or check the FEMA map. Building or repairing in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs a Floodplain Development Permit.

Can I sell a house that was a vacation rental in Rapid City?

Yes. The city has had vacation home zoning rules since December 2025, and registration is open. Buyers may ask for the city registration and the South Dakota lodging license.

When are Pennington County property taxes due?

Taxes are due January 1. The first half is delinquent after April 30 and the second half after October 31.

What happens to deferred homestead taxes when I sell?

The Homestead Exemption defers taxes until the sale, and interest keeps running at a reduced rate. The deferred amount is due at closing.

Selling a house in Aberdeen, South Dakota

Brown County's seat sits in the James River valley, in the northeast corner of the state. Only Sioux Falls and Rapid City are bigger. Slow-moving Moccasin Creek winds through town, and the first Milwaukee Road train rolled in on July 6, 1881, the day the city was founded.

The 2020 census counted 28,495 residents. An estimate for 2025 puts the number at 27,961, which is 1.8 percent under the 2020 base of 28,479. Keep that gentle decline in mind as you weigh a listing price against a cash offer.

Winters and empty houses

Summers run hot and winters run cold and dry. A January day averages 12.8 degrees Fahrenheit, roughly 38 days a year dip below zero, and snow adds up to about 42 inches. Minus 46 in 1912 is the record low.

  • Furnaces fail in cold snaps, and an empty house with no heat can freeze, so keep the thermostat on.
  • Heavy snow tests roofs and gutters.
  • Freeze and thaw swings can crack basement walls and foundations, a favorite subject for home inspectors.

Branches down after a storm? We don't need the yard cleaned up first.

City rules for vacant buildings

If the house sits empty, look first at the city's Nuisance Vacant Building rules. An ordinance declares certain vacant buildings a public nuisance and sets up a registration program, spelling out owner duties, enforcement and penalties. A new registration carries a $1,000 annual fee on the city's fee schedule.

Building Inspection, Code Enforcement and a Residential Contractor Board are also city departments. Phone the city about an empty inherited house to learn if it was flagged and which repairs would lift the flag.

  • Vacant houses can attract code enforcement.
  • A cash buyer can take an inherited or rented house in its present state.
  • Before closing, the title company checks for city charges tied to the property.

Brown County offices

Brown County handles both taxes and recording for Aberdeen. Visit the Treasurer at 25 Market St., Suite 2, Aberdeen, SD 57401, or call (605) 626-7133. Weekday hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., though title transfers can't begin after 4:45 p.m. That office bills property tax for the county, the city, school districts and other taxing districts, and it runs tax aid for low-income and elderly families.

Deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, easements and similar papers are filed with the Register of Deeds, whose land records reach back to the early 1870s. Legal opinions aren't offered there; staff point people to an abstractor, title company or attorney.

Taxes, transfer fee and owner-occupied status

  • Selling triggers a state transfer fee of $0.50 per $500 of value (SDCL 43-4-21) when something of value is exchanged.
  • Tax comes in two halves. Under SDCL 10-21-23, an unpaid first half is delinquent May 1 and an unpaid second half November 1.
  • Owner-occupied status needs a filing with the Director of Equalization by March 15, and you must own and live in the home on November 1.

Aberdeen follows the statewide formula. Market value is assessed, 85 percent of it is taxed, and the bill reflects the combined levy of county, city and school district.

How to appeal your assessment

The state calendar governs appeals, and Brown County posts its dates annually. Assessment notices go out by March 1, with a township informational meeting in early March. After that the pattern is: notice to the local board of equalization about March 12, local boards sitting mid to late March, notice to the county board about April 7, the county board in session April 14 to May 5, and written notice to the Office of Hearing Examiners about May 15.

Court appeals go to circuit court within 30 days of the county board's or hearing examiners' decision. A board that wants to add omitted property or raise an assessment must tell the owner when and where, so the owner can show up or mail proof.

What closing looks like

After you accept an offer, a title company reviews ownership, requests the tax payoff from the Brown County Treasurer and prepares the deed. The state transfer fee and recording are handled at closing, and the deed is filed with the Register of Deeds. Whatever tax is still unpaid comes out of your proceeds.

Timing matters in this county. Taxes come due in two halves, and an unpaid first half turns delinquent on May 1, an unpaid second half on November 1. A title transfer must be started before 4:45 p.m. at the Treasurer, so aim to finish paperwork early in the day. If the house is inherited, the signer must be the person with authority over the estate.

Preparing a house for an as-is sale

A cash sale doesn't call for a deep clean or a paint job, but a few small steps still help. Keep the heat on through winter, because frozen pipes cost more than a month of gas. Clear the walkway of snow so we or an inspector can reach the door. Gather any warranties or permit papers, and write down anything you already know is broken, such as a failing furnace or a leaking basement wall.

If belongings are left behind, tell us. We can usually take the house with contents in place, which spares you a cleanout. If a tenant lives there, we can talk about whether they stay or move out on a date that works for everyone. Whatever the situation, tell us early and we will work around it. A short phone call or a few photos usually lets us give a written offer quickly, and nothing is final until you accept it.

Your options for a fast sale

Three paths are open: an agent, a sale by owner, or cash. Listing may fetch the top price, yet it relies on showings, a buyer's loan, an appraisal and repair demands. A cash deal drops those steps and leaves the closing day to you.

We purchase Aberdeen homes as-is. You pay no commission, repair bills or closing costs, and our written offer can sit beside a listing for comparison. Send the address and basics on the house and its occupants; once we have seen it, the choice is yours.

Before talking to any buyer, collect the deed, the newest tax statement and a mortgage payoff if there is one. Landlords add the lease. With an inherited house, decide who signs. The county supplies the tax payoff, and a title company confirms nothing else clings to the property.

How many people live in Aberdeen, SD?

About 27,961 as of July 1, 2025, which is down 1.8% from the April 2020 estimate base of 28,479.

What is the median home value in Aberdeen?

Owner-occupied homes had a median value of $217,300 for 2020-2024, and owners live in 61.7% of homes.

Which office do I call about Aberdeen property taxes?

The Brown County Treasurer, (605) 626-7133, 25 Market St., Suite 2. A question about value goes to the Brown County Director of Equalization.

What is the South Dakota transfer fee when I sell?

Fifty cents per $500 of value, equal to $1.00 per $1,000, set by SDCL 43-4-21 and charged on a deed involving consideration.

Can I sell a vacant Aberdeen house as-is?

Yes. Ask the city about Nuisance Vacant Building registration first, and then an as-is cash sale needs no repairs or showings.

Brookings housing at a glance

Brookings sits 60 miles up Interstate 29 from Sioux Falls and serves as the Brookings County seat. Its population was 23,377 in the 2020 census. South Dakota State University had 12,065 students in fall 2024 and employs more people than anyone else in town, so home sales here rise and fall with the school year.

Near campus you will find duplexes, older single-family houses and student rentals. Toward the edge of town the neighborhoods are mostly family homes. Plenty of sellers are people who inherited a rental or spent years leasing to students, and they are left with scuffed floors, tired kitchens and a tenant whose lease ends on a set day. Unemployment was 2.5 percent in December 2024, which helps buyer demand, but a house that needs heavy work still sits.

Rules for rental houses

The city's Code Enforcement office inspects rentals and issues the rental license. One license can run up to four years, or whatever an ordinance requires, and it caps how many people may live in each unit.

  • Apply with the Rental Housing Permit Application.
  • Tenants worried about crowding can file the city's complaint form.
  • Fee questions go to Code Enforcement at (605) 692-6629.

Landlords who plan to sell should look up the license expiration date and the occupant cap now. Anyone buying with tenants in place will want both. An expired license or an unresolved inspection note costs less to clear while you own the house than it does in the middle of a contract.

Pull out the lease as well. An end date, a security deposit that has to change hands, or a tenant who refuses showings will all affect when the house can close.

Payments go through the counter, the mail, the county website or a drop box on the building's west side. A counter payment by credit card adds a 2.5 percent service fee. The treasurer will not take a partial payment against taxes that are due or delinquent.

The office also administers the Disabled Veteran and Surviving Spouse exemption and the Senior Citizens and Disabled assessment freeze. Owners who receive either one should ask the staff what a sale does to the benefit before putting the house on the market.

At closing, the title company normally takes the unpaid part of the current bill out of your proceeds. Request a payoff amount ahead of time so the settlement statement holds no surprises.

Flood risk near the creeks

Houses close to a creek deserve a second look. The city's Engineering Division has pages on floodplains and on the Six-Mile Creek flood risk mitigation work, and the future land use map shows the Six Mile Creek and Deer Creek floodplains.

FEMA draws the floodplain line. Enter your parcel on FEMA's map or ask the engineering staff if your lot falls inside. Buyers ask this question, and the state disclosure form includes a line about flood plains, so you will be putting an answer on paper either way.

Winter wear on a Brookings house

Winters in Brookings are long and cold, with lows under zero on about 35 days a year and snowfall near 35.8 inches. Furnaces, water heaters and old pipes take the abuse first. Spring melt then puts sump pumps and basement walls to the test.

Home inspectors in town tend to check the age of the furnace, the shape of the windows and any sign of water downstairs. If you already know what they will find, you can negotiate from strength. A furnace tune-up and a cleared-out basement are cheap ways to get there.

The register of deeds will not record your deed unless a Certificate of Real Estate Value, form PT 56, comes with it. The Brookings County Register of Deeds can give you its own recording fee and the transfer amount for your deal.

From first call to closing day

Here is how a direct sale runs. You describe the house and we visit it. An offer follows. If you accept, a title company or attorney confirms who owns the property, clears any liens and drafts the closing documents. You sign, the deed is recorded, and the money reaches you.

Collect a few items before our visit: the deed or legal description, your most recent tax notice, any mortgage payoff information and a plain list of what is broken. Students leave in a rush each spring, so when tenants are moving out, schedule the walk-through after they have gone. For an inherited house, have the papers that show who is allowed to sign.

Back taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at the table. You do not need to find the cash beforehand.

When does a cash sale make sense in Brookings?

Cash works for owners who value speed or who would rather not fix up and stage a house. The usual cases are inherited homes, beat-up student rentals and houses with years of put-off maintenance.

We buy Brookings houses as-is, so you make no repairs, and you owe nothing if you turn the offer down. You skip photos, open houses, a buyer's mortgage approval and the repair list an inspector writes. The closing date is yours to choose, and many sellers pick a date that fits a move or a lease ending.

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in Brookings, SD?

The 2020 census counted 23,377 residents. The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 25,355.

Do Brookings rental houses need a license?

Yes. Code Enforcement inspects rentals and issues licenses that last up to four years, with an occupant cap for each unit.

When are property taxes due in Brookings County?

April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second. Special assessments and bills under $50 must be paid in full by April 30.

Can I pay Brookings County taxes online?

Yes. The county takes card, PayPal or e-check online, plus counter, mail and drop-box payments. A card at the counter adds a 2.5 percent fee.

Does a Brookings seller need a disclosure form, and what is the PT 56?

Yes, South Dakota sellers must give the buyer the property condition disclosure. The PT 56 is the Certificate of Real Estate Value, listing buyer, seller, legal description, price and terms, and a deed cannot be recorded without it.
